extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, government officials, NGOs, researchers, and members of the public interested in designing or evaluating public consultations
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing, running, and evaluating public consultation processes (town halls, public comment periods, deliberative assemblies, surveys, participatory budgeting) with attention to representativeness, notification, deliberation, and legal/procedural features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification (publicize the matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation usually involves notification (to publicize the matter to be consulted on).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notification methods include posting a notice of completion in the newspaper, on the web, and mailing to known interested parties (designated as 'stakeholders' or 'interested parties'). Notification is a distinct step prior to consultation to publicize the matter under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation as two-way flow of information
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultation (a two-way flow of information and opinion exchange) between the government/organisers and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective consultation should enable exchange rather than one-way information delivery; methods vary but all involve providing background information and an opportunity for deliberation on the regulation, law or plan under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation (involving stakeholders in drafting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation involves stakeholders in the drafting of policy or legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation goes beyond being consulted to involving stakeholders directly in drafting; it is one of the trio of typical stages in consultation: notification, consultation, and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of background information
rubrics_metrics.description: All consultation methods involve the provision of background information on the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background materials should be supplied so participants can deliberate knowledgeably; for surveys and deliberative exercises, respondents are provided relevant briefing materials and arguments for and against various proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness: self-selected vs representative samples
rubrics_metrics.description: A key dividing line is whether participants are self-selected or a representative sample of the population; only representative samples allow characterizing the distribution of views in the general population and identifying majority views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve a representative sample, the ideal is purely random selection. Reasonably representative samples can be achieved by opt-in samples that are stratified in advance and weighted afterwards according to key demographic variables, and by ensuring the universe of potential respondents does not have evident biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling methods and requirements for mini-publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative samples for deliberative groups are often achieved by random selection (sortition) to form 'mini-publics' such as deliberative polls, citizens' juries, and citizens' assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberative assemblies typically brief participants with experts, allow discussion, and culminate in a vote or recommendation. Citizens' juries are small (several dozen) meeting for several intensive days; citizens' assemblies are larger (100–500) and may meet across days or sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment period and record
rubrics_metrics.description: A public comment period is established and comments received by the cutoff date become part of the official public record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is typically a notice of completion of a draft (e.g., environmental impact report) which is posted and mailed; some statutes mandate that comments be replied to or incorporated into the final document. Government portals may allow review of comments and searching by keyword, providing commentators an opportunity to view others' remarks before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement to reply or incorporate comments (where statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases, there is a statutory mandate that those comments be replied to or incorporated in some fashion into the Final document in advance of the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When present, such mandates give commentators an opportunity to see how comments are addressed and may influence the final decision or documentation; agencies may be required to respond to substantive points raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public meetings vs public hearings (openness and selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public meetings (e.g., town halls) are open to all, whereas public hearings are not open to all and participants may be selected by the governing body due to expertise or representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should choose the format appropriate to the goal: broad access (town halls) versus targeted expert/stakeholder input (hearings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative opinion polling (combine survey + face-to-face deliberation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberative opinion polling combines surveys of a representative sample with face-to-face deliberation: sample surveyed in advance, provided briefing materials and expert presentations, participate in deliberation, then resurveyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically uses a sample of several hundred; the approach aims to measure how informed deliberation changes preferences (developed by James Fishkin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public consultation surveys (fully deliberative within survey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation surveys conduct the entirety of the deliberative process within the survey: respondents receive briefing materials and arguments for and against proposals and then provide a final recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usually done with large representative samples (several thousand nationally and several hundred subnationally); can be used as basis for face-to-face forums and to inform legislators about constituent preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participatory budgeting design and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Participatory budgeting involves ordinary people, sometimes representative, making decisions about a government's budget through democratic deliberation and decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frameworks vary widely in scale, procedure, and objective; many designs are contextualized to local conditions. Participatory budgeting can be legally enforced or promoted by NGOs and has been implemented in many municipalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for viewing others' comments (transparency tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a government portal which may allow review of comments and opportunity for making comment and can be searched by keyword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portals increase transparency and let commentators view and react to others' remarks; they support accountability and public record-keeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of unrepresentativeness and demographic skew
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation meetings tend to be unrepresentative of the general population, often dominated by older, wealthier, whiter residents and homeowners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisers should be aware of likely participation biases and consider methods (representative sampling, outreach, weighting) to mitigate such domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for consultation to hinder or delay projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Public consultation is controversial for its role in hindering and delaying development and infrastructure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planners should balance participatory aims with project timelines and anticipate that consultation can be used to slow or block proposals; design processes to manage delay risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Arnstein's ladder to assess levels of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnstein's ladder is a frequently used tool for understanding different levels of community participation in consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware some academics contest its universal applicability; it remains a common heuristic to distinguish tokenism from meaningful power-sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding against illegitimate/AI-generated feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated text (such as from bots on social media) may result in illegitimate feedback in addition to legitimate testimony and opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisers should be cautious of automated or synthetic submissions and consider verification, filtering, or provenance checks to protect the integrity of the consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of government manipulation or biased question framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments can misuse consultations by sending suggestive questions or framing that push an agenda (example: national consultations with leading/suggestive questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must ensure neutrality and avoid leading language; independent oversight and clear question design help prevent manipulation. Be aware of examples where consultative mechanisms have been used for propaganda or mass messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/regulatory timing requirements (example: mandatory consultation periods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions legally mandate consultation periods (example: Sweden has a mandatory consultation period of three months for all proposed major legislation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consultation design must comply with statutory timelines and procedural rules; legal mandates can determine minimum notice and comment durations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and context sensitivity of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Frameworks and methods differ throughout the globe in terms of scale, procedure, and objective; many consultation designs are contextualized to local conditions and needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose methods (surveys, mini-publics, town halls, participatory budgeting) appropriate to the policy question, scale, and local political/legal context.
